title: Self-Play: The One Loop That Already Closed

questions.question: Why does the lesson call AlphaZero (Silver et al., 2018) a fully closed improvement loop?
options: Its network was large enough to memorise every position reached during its training runs
It generated its own games, the rules scored them exactly, and its opponent was its current self
Human grandmaster games were filtered by Elo rating and replayed until the network matched them
A separate judge model rewarded moves that resembled expert play in Go, chess and shogi
questions.explanation: Closure means data, verification and curriculum all come from inside the loop: self-play supplies games, the game rules score them without error, and the current policy is its own opponent.

questions.question: Which closure condition does an open-ended domain such as research or essay writing fail first, according to the lesson?
options: Condition 2: no process generates new tasks at the learner's current frontier
Condition 3: the deployment distribution drifts away from the training games
Condition 1: no verifier exists that the policy cannot game
None: open-ended domains satisfy all three once enough data is available
questions.explanation: There is no function that returns win/draw/loss for a research idea or an essay; any judge or rubric standing in for one can be optimised against, which is the Lesson 14 problem.

questions.question: In code/main.py the verifier flips who won with probability p. Why does this hurt the learner more than simply adding variance?
options: Flips make draws impossible to learn, so the learner can never settle on the minimax value
Noisy wins reward refutable lines, and the max in the Q update turns that noise into overestimates
The flips change which player moves first, which breaks the alternation of seats in training
The noise erases the Q-table at the end of every generation, so nothing carries over
questions.explanation: Draws are never flipped, so a safe draw stays at exactly 0 while risky lines receive occasional false +1s; the max over noisy estimates is biased upward, so the policy keeps choosing lines a minimax opponent refutes.

questions.question: In generational self-play, what does the exploit column (loss rate against the worst past generation) diagnose?
options: Cycling or forgetting: the new policy beats its parent but an older generation still refutes it
Overfitting to the minimax opponent that the evaluation games use after every generation
How much the Q-table grew between two consecutive generations of the same learner
Whether the corrupted verifier flipped more results in later generations than early ones
questions.explanation: Measuring only against the parent hides rock-paper-scissors dynamics; a non-zero loss rate against an archived generation means progress was not transitive, which population-based training is meant to fix.

questions.question: AlphaProof (DeepMind, 2024) is presented as the first transfer of the self-play recipe outside games. What played the role of the game rules?
options: A fine-tuned Gemini model that graded candidate proofs for readability
Human IMO coordinators scoring each submitted proof out of seven points
The Lean proof assistant, which accepts or rejects a formal proof
A majority vote over several independently sampled candidate proofs
questions.explanation: Lean checks every proof step mechanically, so a found proof is correct by construction; Gemini was used to autoformalise problem statements, not to score proofs.

questions.question: Silver and Sutton's 'Era of Experience' (2025) argues that experience-driven learning generalises beyond games. Which objection does the lesson raise?
options: Experience streams would need more compute than any lab can afford this decade
Lifelong agents forget early experience, so the stream must be replayed in full
Non-human reasoning cannot be audited, so the loop must stay human-in-the-loop
Grounded rewards exist for games and proofs; most target domains offer only gameable proxies
questions.explanation: The thesis stands or falls on grounded rewards (closure condition 1); where the only available signal is a learned judge or a human proxy, the loop optimises the proxy, as Lessons 06 and 14 show.
